analysis.one_liner: Forces concentrated hospitals to charge Medicare rates to all patients, publish prices, and face tougher merger scrutiny.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote or a hearing in any committee; its price-limit and transparency requirements never took effect.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required hospitals in markets with little competition to charge every patient — not just Medicare beneficiaries — the Medicare rate for their services, and to publish what they charge for the 100 most common hospital procedures. It also would have paid Medicare patients the same whether they are treated in a hospital-owned clinic or a private doctor's office, given the Federal Trade Commission $160 million to investigate hospital mergers, and rewarded states that remove rules restricting competition. It was referred to three House committees in January 2019 and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who are privately insured or uninsured would see the biggest gains: in areas where one or a few hospital systems dominate, those hospitals would have to charge them Medicare rates instead of the much higher prices they currently negotiate with insurers, and would have to post their prices publicly. Medicare taxpayers would save from site-neutral payment, which pays the same for a service whether it happens in a hospital-owned clinic or a doctor's office. Taxpayers also gain from more FTC scrutiny of hospital mergers that tend to raise prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Privately insured and uninsured hospital patients

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals in highly concentrated markets (measured by a market-concentration index) would have to charge all patients — including the privately insured and the uninsured — Medicare rates, directly attacking the markup hospitals charge private payers.
Hospitals would have to publicly post their actual prices for the 100 most-used hospital services, in a standardized federal system, so patients could comparison-shop.
Medicare would pay the same for a service whether it is delivered in a hospital-owned clinic or an independent doctor's office, removing the premium patients and taxpayers pay for the hospital label.

The FTC would get $160 million in dedicated funding to investigate anti-competitive hospital mergers, and states that free up provider competition (no certificate-of-need laws, broader scope of practice for nurses) could win federal infrastructure grants.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals in concentrated markets would lose the ability to charge privately insured and uninsured patients well above Medicare rates — a major revenue cut. Physician groups in Medicare accountable care organizations would lose shared-savings bonus payments. Physicians who own hospitals would gain expansion rights, but consolidated hospitals bear the main cost.

drawbacks.text: Forcing concentrated hospitals to charge everyone Medicare rates would cut their revenue sharply, and critics of rate-setting argue this could reduce services or push costs onto Medicare itself if private-pay rates end up cross-subsidizing government rates.

The bill repeals the shared-savings bonuses in Medicare's accountable care program, removing a financial incentive for provider groups to coordinate and lower costs — a trade-off an honest supporter would have to defend.

Repealing the Stark-law limits on physician-owned hospital expansion could re-open a loophole that health policy researchers have linked to higher utilization, since physicians who own a facility profit from referring patients to it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits are potentially large: hospitals with market power would face hard price limits and disclosure requirements, and regulators would get more resources to challenge consolidation. The costs are real but manageable: hospitals in concentrated markets would take a revenue cut, physicians in shared-savings programs would lose bonuses, and physicians who own hospitals could expand and gain a competitive tool. The bill never received committee consideration, so its technical workability was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and their subcommittees in early 2019, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 11, 2019 and referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary Committees.
It was then referred to subcommittees on Health and on Antitrust in January and February 2019.
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded; the last action was the February-March 2019 subcommittee referrals.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospital systems with local market power kept charging privately insured and uninsured patients rates far above Medicare rates, and avoided new price-transparency and antitrust obligations.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only two Republican supporters and no Democratic cosponsors, and because it never got a hearing or vote, no roll call shows where either party stood.

industries.note: Hospitals in concentrated markets would be forced to charge privately insured and uninsured patients Medicare rates, eliminating the private-pay markups that drive much of their revenue, and would have to publish prices. Their interests in this bill run directly against patients paying hospital prices.

industries.industry: Physician groups in Medicare accountable care organizations
industries.note: The bill repeals the shared-savings bonus payments that reward provider groups for cutting Medicare costs, taking away their extra revenue stream.
Repealing the Affordable Care Act's Stark-law provisions would let physician-owned hospitals expand capacity again, ending a restriction that limited their growth since 2010.

Lower hospital prices would reduce insurers' claims costs, but the bill also bars states that let insurers steer patients to lower-cost options... states whose 'any willing provider' laws are struck from their books qualify for grants, indirectly pressuring insurers' network arrangements.
The bill authorizes $160 million for FTC staff to investigate anti-competitive hospital mergers and practices.
